screeningSummary: Certified approach controller asks how she'd tell a drone from a UAP on her scope BEFORE it happens
arcNotes: Question arc, technical info: drones have manners (slow, low, hover, die mid-pattern on battery); UAP cases break physics (track jumps at refresh rate, impossible descents, never go home). She has a track strip from years ago - Vern sends her to file it

lines.text: All the time. Little returns near the field, drifting, hovering in the wind sometimes - you learn to ignore them. What scares me is that the ignoring is a habit. That the real one, if it ever comes, will be wearing the same shape.
lines.voiceText: All the time, man. Little returns near the field, drifting, hovering in the wind sometimes - you learn to ignore them. What scares me is that the ignoring is a habit, you know? That the real one, if it ever comes, will be wearing the same shape, uh... the same shape.

lines.text: Then let me hand you the habit-breaker. Drones have manners: they're slow - usually under a hundred knots. They're low - under four hundred feet. They hover, they drift, they fly grids, and they go home when the battery dies - they vanish mid-pattern. That's their signature: a return that holds position in a headwind, or dies in the middle of a grid. The cases say the other kind has no manners at all: descents from flight levels your scope shouldn't hold, accelerations that outrun the antenna refresh - that's your track jumps and your split plots - and they never go home. So here's the rule for your sector: a return breaking the rules is a drone. A return breaking physics is a report.

lines.text: The discriminator: drones exhibit characteristic behavior - velocities typically under one hundred knots, altitudes under four hundred feet, hovering, grid patterns, and mid-pattern disappearance at battery exhaustion. Signature: position-holding returns in headwind, or returns terminating mid-grid. Anomalous cases exhibit none of these: descents from beyond scope ceiling, accelerations exceeding antenna refresh rate - manifesting as track jumps and plot splitting - and no return-to-base. Operational rule: rule-breaking returns classify as drones; physics-breaking returns classify as reports.

lines.text: You kept the strip - of course you did; you're one of the careful ones. So do this: copy it, write the date, the shift, the sector, and send it to an investigator network. A controller's track strip is worth a hundred phone videos, and the networks know it. Keep the original safe - not photographed, filed. And someday, when somebody official asks whether anyone at your facility has ever seen an anomalous return, your strip is the answer - and you won't have to decide after the fact whether you saw it. You already decided. You kept it.
